title: Mira's treasure
hookLine: a woman who left a palace counts her treasure: the name of God
carry: the name of God is the real treasure
tomorrow: Chaitanya takes the names to the street

cards: A strange inventory for a princess. Mira grew up, the stories say, among jewels and silks, in a house with a treasury. She walked away from all of it.
And one of the songs sung in her voice is about getting rich. Payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo. I've found it, I've found the treasure, the jewel of Ram's name.
A woman who left a royal house describes what she has now in the language of money.

teach.h: READ IT LIKE A BANK STATEMENT.
teach.b: Listen to it like a bank statement. Credit: a priceless thing, given to me by my true guru, out of kindness. Balance: the savings of lifetime after lifetime, found at last.
Then come terms no bank has ever offered.
Spend it, and it doesn't run down. Thieves can't touch it. Day by day it grows.

Then the song leaves the bank for a river. The boat is truth, the boatman is the true guru, and I have crossed the ocean of becoming. The last line: Mira's lord is Giridhar, and she sings his praise with joy upon joy.
So what is the treasure? Not a thing. A name.

teach.h: NAMA: THE NAME IS THE TREASURE.
teach.b: This is one of the great teachings of bhakti: the name of God, nama, isn't a label stuck on the treasure. For the bhakti saints, saying the name is how you hold it.

teach.h: JAPA: THE NAME, AGAIN AND AGAIN.
teach.b: That's why so many Hindus repeat a name of God, softly, again and again, often on a mala, a string of a hundred and eight beads. It's called japa. Notice the names here, too.
Mira's beloved is Krishna, the mountain-lifter, yet she sings of the jewel of Ram's name. Some readers hear Ram's name here as the name of God itself, and the song holds both names without strain.
And the treasure is given, not earned: a guru hands it over in kindness.

teach.h: THE ONE THING THAT GROWS WHEN SPENT.
teach.b: So a woman who lost a palace counts herself rich, because the name of God is the one thing that grows when it's spent.

how: Payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo is sung as a bhajan at home gatherings, in temples and on concert stages, and many Hindus practice japa, repeating a name of God on a mala of 108 beads.

o: songs sung in Mira's voice, here of the jewel of the name
songs Tulsidas wrote in praise of Ram's name
royal songs counting the treasures of Mewar's palace

p: the name of God, Mira's treasure
repeating the name, bead by bead

s: Mira sings that the treasure runs down as she spends it
spending doesn't use it up, thieves can't steal it, and it grows day by day.
in the song, the treasure is a gift from a guru
japa means repeating a name of God, often on a mala
a string of 108 beads, one name for each bead: the treasure Mira sings of, spent and growing.

games.q: you've left a palace and its treasury behind. someone asks what you have now. what do you say?
o: nothing, and I've made my peace with it.
a treasure: the jewel of the name, and it grows when spent.
games.why: payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo: I've found the treasure. in Mira's ledger the palace is the small loss, and the name of God is the fortune.

practice: Today, try japa, the practice this song is about. Choose a name of God your family uses, Ram, Krishna, Shiva, the Mother, or simply Om, and say it softly, once with each slow breath.
If you have a mala, move one bead for each name; if not, count on your fingers. Notice that saying it doesn't use anything up.
If you don't pray, repeat one word that holds what you love most, and let it be your treasure for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Mirabai's songs. In this one, the jewel of the name: a treasure no thief can steal, which grows each day it's spent.

orig.note: Hindi, in Devanagari: a jewel. Ram ratan dhan is the treasure of the jewel of Ram's name.

carryVoice: Your line: the name of God is the real treasure. Spend it, and it grows. That's day nine hundred thirty-two.

sources.ref: Padavali of Mirabai, the song 'Payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo'
